clinicalPearls: Acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish (often as fermented or pickled fish dishes) that carry metacercariae; highly endemic across parts of Southeast Asia and eastern Europe
Most light infections are asymptomatic; heavier or chronic infection causes right upper quadrant discomfort, dyspepsia, hepatomegaly and features of biliary irritation
Chronic infection is a recognised risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma, making it one of the few parasitic causes of a defined human cancer
Diagnosis rests on finding characteristic operculated eggs in stool, which are difficult to distinguish from other opisthorchiid and heterophyid eggs on morphology alone
Peripheral eosinophilia is common, and imaging may show intrahepatic ductal dilatation, gallbladder sludge and biliary wall thickening
Praziquantel is the treatment of choice and is highly effective against the adult flukes
Public health control depends on discouraging consumption of raw freshwater fish and on sanitation to interrupt egg contamination of water bodies
reference.pathophysiology: Opisthorchis species are small liver flukes whose life cycle involves freshwater snails as first intermediate hosts and cyprinid fish as second intermediate hosts. Humans and other fish-eating mammals become definitive hosts when they ingest infective metacercariae in raw or inadequately cooked fish. The larvae excyst in the duodenum, ascend the biliary tree through the ampulla, and mature into adult flukes residing in the intrahepatic bile ducts and gallbladder. Long-standing mechanical irritation and the fluke's secretions drive chronic inflammation, epithelial hyperplasia, periductal fibrosis and cholestasis; sustained biliary injury with proliferative and dysplastic change underlies the strong association with cholangiocarcinoma. Eggs passed in bile reach the intestine and are excreted in faeces, continuing the cycle when they contaminate freshwater.
additionalDifferentials: Clonorchiasis (Clonorchis sinensis), which is clinically and morphologically very similar
Fascioliasis and other biliary trematode infection
Cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis with biliary colic
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites, ideally with concentration and repeated samples
Serology or antigen detection where available to support diagnosis in light infection
Full blood count for eosinophilia and liver function tests
Abdominal ultrasound for biliary dilatation, gallbladder sludge and ductal wall changes
MRCP or CT when malignancy or complicated biliary disease is suspected
Endoscopic examination of bile with cytology if cholangiocarcinoma is a concern
redFlags: Progressive jaundice, weight loss and a biliary mass suggesting cholangiocarcinoma
Fever with rigors and right upper quadrant pain indicating ascending cholangitis
Biliary obstruction with worsening liver dysfunction
Recurrent cholangitis or intrahepatic stone formation
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated infection responds well to anthelmintic treatment with resolution of symptoms, but chronic heavy infection carries a serious long-term risk of cholangiocarcinoma and biliary complications, for which the outlook is poor.
pitfalls: Assuming eradication removes cancer risk; malignancy can develop years after treatment in previously heavily infected patients
Misidentifying eggs as heterophyid or other opisthorchiid species because of overlapping morphology
Missing light infections on a single stool sample and prematurely excluding the diagnosis
Attributing biliary symptoms solely to gallstones and overlooking coexistent fluke infection in endemic populations
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Give praziquantel as the anthelmintic of choice, being highly effective against the adult liver flukes, with albendazole as an alternative
Educate patients to avoid raw, undercooked, fermented or pickled freshwater fish to eliminate the source and prevent reinfection
Provide symptomatic relief of biliary discomfort and dyspepsia
Undertake long-term surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma with imaging in chronic or heavy infection, given the established malignant risk
Manage biliary complications such as cholangitis or obstruction with endoscopic drainage and antibiotics
Confirm cure with follow-up stool examination for ova
Refer to hepatobiliary and oncology services when malignancy or complicated biliary disease is suspected
